videos.displayTitle: The Promise of an Understandable Intelligence
videos.summary: The series opens in legacy LS20. Yannick introduces his aim for SRA: an agent whose perceptions, hypotheses, explorations, and conclusions are available for inspection. ARC-AGI 3 provides unfamiliar worlds in which the meaning of an action has to be discovered. The episode explains why he chose symbolic representations to express those discoveries, and how the agent’s own reasoning could become something both the system and its developer can examine.

fullText.author: Yannick Fontan
fullText.text:
Symbolic Reasoning Agent
An experimental journey through ARC-AGI 3
Episode 1 • Legacy Game LS20
The Promise of an Understandable Intelligence,
 Or How to Think Outside the Black Box.

For decades, we have asked artificial intelligence to produce the right answers.
But what if we have been asking the wrong question?
What if the real challenge is not producing the right answer...
...but understanding why it is the right answer?
We are entering an era in which machines can predict, complete, generate, and optimize with extraordinary efficiency.
Yet one fundamental question remains.
Do they truly understand what they are doing?
Or are they simply recognizing statistical regularities hidden within an ocean of data?
I believe the next revolution in artificial intelligence will not be a revolution of scale.
It will be a revolution of understanding.
A truly intelligent system should not only be capable of acting.
It should also be capable of explaining its reasoning.
Visible to itself.
Visible to human beings.
Visible to those who will one day have to trust it.
Because an intelligence that cannot explain its reasoning remains a black box, no matter how impressive its performance.

What you are seeing on the screen today is an environment from ARC-AGI 3.
ARC is a collection of small interactive worlds created by François Chollet to explore one fundamental question:
How can an intelligence learn to understand an entirely new world?
There are no natural language instructions.
No predefined knowledge.
No explanations.
Only an unfamiliar environment.
Observe.
Explore.
Understand.
For many researchers, ARC is simply a benchmark.
For me, it is something much more profound.
It is a laboratory for understanding.

For the past several months, I have been using this laboratory to explore a different path.
A path that does not merely seek the correct answer.
A path that seeks to make reasoning itself visible.
This path has a name.
Symbolic reasoning.
Symbolic reasoning is not about finding statistical correlations.
It is about manipulating concepts.
Building hypotheses.
Discovering relationships.
Planning exploration.
Drawing conclusions.
Learning from evidence.
And above all...
explaining why an action makes sense.
I believe this capability will become essential if we hope to build artificial intelligence that deserves our trust.

The project I am presenting today is therefore not simply an attempt to solve ARC puzzles.
It is an attempt to build an architecture where every perception can become a concept.
Every concept a belief.
Every belief a hypothesis.
Every hypothesis an exploration.
And every exploration new knowledge.
An architecture where reasoning no longer disappears behind millions, or even trillions, of parameters.
An architecture where reasoning becomes...
Observable.
Manipulable.
Verifiable.
And ultimately...
Understandable.

This series of videos will document that construction.
Step by step.
From the first foundations to a complete symbolic reasoning architecture.
I am not claiming to present an Artificial General Intelligence today.
I am proposing something more fundamental.
The beginning of an exploration into what it truly means...
to understand.
Because I believe that intelligence should not be measured solely by its ability to predict.
It should also be measured by its ability to make its own reasoning intelligible.
And I believe one of the greatest challenges of our generation is precisely this:
To make artificial intelligence understandable.

True science is not the one that predicts. It is the one that explains.

videos.title: ARC AGI 3 SRA Ep 2 LS20 Official
videos.summary: Official LS20 is the setting for Human-Agent Principle Distillation. An SRA run produces evidence about where its reasoning stops being sufficient. Yannick examines that evidence and identifies a principle that could apply more broadly. A coding agent integrates the principle, and the next run tests its use. The episode describes this development cycle and the need to connect new knowledge to existing structure so that it can support later discoveries.

fullText.author: Yannick Fontan
fullText.text:
Symbolic Reasoning Agent
An experimental journey through ARC-AGI 3
Episode 2 • Official Game LS20
Human-Agent Principle Distillation

Last time, I introduced the vision behind this project.
Today, I would like to challenge one of the most influential definitions of intelligence.
François Chollet defines intelligence as the ability to efficiently adapt to new situations.
I believe this definition can be pushed one step further.
Because if a situation were truly, completely unknown...
No familiar concepts.
No familiar relationships.
No familiar principles.
...then no intelligence could solve it efficiently.
It would have no choice but to explore almost blindly.
So when an intelligence adapts elegantly to something new...
I don't believe it is because the situation is completely unknown.
I believe it is because something inside that situation is already familiar.
Not the situation itself.
Its underlying structure.

This leads me to a slightly different definition.
Intelligence is having both a rich enough structure of meaning and the ability to navigate it, so that every new situation can be connected to it and experienced as familiar.
Knowledge alone is not enough.
A dictionary contains knowledge.
It does not understand.
Intelligence requires structure.
Relationships.
Hierarchy.
Meaning.
And above all...
The ability to create new connections.

This is exactly what today's video is about.
As the agent explores this new version of LS20, it eventually reaches a situation it cannot solve.
That failure is not the end of the reasoning process.
It is the beginning.
Together, the human and the agent analyze what happened.
Not to invent a solution for this particular level...
...but to extract a general principle.
A principle that could apply to many future worlds.
I call this process Human-Agent Principle Distillation.
Here is the loop: The symbolic reasoning agent executes and produces evidence. The human identifies a new principle. The coding agent integrates that principle into the architecture. And the cycle begins again.  
The goal is never to memorize a solution.
The goal is to discover a reusable principle.
Once that principle enters the symbolic knowledge base...
The architecture itself becomes richer.
Its structure of meaning expands.
And tomorrow...
Another unknown world becomes just a little more familiar.

This is not simply learning.
It is the continuous construction of a structure of meaning.
One principle at a time.
One world at a time.
One abstraction at a time.
Because I believe that intelligence does not grow by accumulating experiences.
It grows by organizing them into an ever more coherent structure of meaning.

"Every new principle makes tomorrow's unknown a little more familiar."

videos.title: ARC AGI 3 SRA Ep 3
videos.summary: In the LP85 environment, Yannick introduces Operational Artificial Consciousness as a maintained account of what currently matters to the agent: beliefs, objectives, principles, hypotheses, resources, and their relationships. Observations and deductions update that state. Its practical purpose is continuity across successive reasoning steps, with current commitments and priorities available for inspection. The episode also considers self-observation and revision as possible extensions of this operational definition.

fullText.author: Yannick Fontan
fullText.text:
Symbolic Reasoning Agent
An experimental journey through ARC-AGI 3
Episode 3 • Game LP85
Operational Artificial Consciousness 
Beyond the Modern Definition of Consciousness

Last time, I proposed a different definition of intelligence.

Today, I would like to challenge another concept that I believe has become increasingly restrictive over the past decades: the modern definition of consciousness itself.

Discussions about consciousness are largely dominated by one question: does an entity possess subjective experience? Can it feel? Does it experience what philosophers call qualia? 
These are fascinating philosophical questions. However, I believe that by gradually reducing consciousness to this single dimension, modern science has unintentionally narrowed a concept that was historically much richer, and in doing so may have slowed scientific progress toward artificial consciousness.

For most of human history, consciousness referred not only to subjective experience, but also to awareness, self-knowledge, discernment, wisdom, moral judgment and, more fundamentally, the ability to remain aligned with the principles that give meaning and direction to one's existence.

I believe this broader conception provides a far more useful foundation for artificial intelligence.

If consciousness is defined exclusively by subjective experience, we quickly reach a scientific impasse.. Subjective experience cannot be directly observed or experimentally verified. An artificial system could progressively understand itself, monitor its own reasoning, preserve coherent beliefs and long-term objectives, yet we would still declare it non-conscious because we cannot answer an inherently private philosophical question.

Rather than beginning with the hardest philosophical problem, I propose beginning with what can actually be engineered.

This is what I call Operational Artificial Consciousness.

Operational consciousness is the continuous maintenance of the internal state of everything that currently matters: beliefs, objectives, principles, hypotheses, available resources and the relationships connecting them.

I summarize this with a simple definition:

Operational consciousness is the continuous reading and writing of the state of everything that matters.

Within my architecture, consciousness is not another reasoning engine. It is the symbolic structure that preserves the continuity of reasoning itself. Every observation updates it. Every deduction reorganizes it. Every newly distilled principle enriches it. Without this continuously maintained internal state, reasoning becomes fragmented and intelligence gradually loses its coherence.

I also believe that consciousness is better understood as a spectrum than as a binary property. A first level maintains awareness of the current situation. Higher levels may observe their own reasoning, question their own principles and eventually repair themselves. Whether subjective experience ultimately emerges from such an architecture remains an open question. My claim is simply that these operational forms of consciousness are a necessary foundation upon which any richer notion of consciousness would almost certainly have to be built.

The objective of this project is therefore not simply to build a machine that solves problems, but one capable of knowing what it believes at every moment, why it believes it, what deserves its attention and how its own understanding evolves over time.

As Rabelais wrote: “Science without conscience is but the ruin of the soul.” I would simply add: “Intelligence should first be guided by its consciousness.”

videos.title: ARC AGI 3 SRA Ep 4
videos.summary: This episode uses official FT09 to examine how a human solver identifies and describes their own reasoning. Yannick discusses the geometric perception, inference, analogy, and hypothesis testing that can pass unnoticed within an intuitive decision. Verbalizing those steps exposes their assumptions and structure. It is part of the development method introduced in Episode 2: extracting a reusable principle first requires a sufficiently clear account of the reasoning behind it.

fullText.author: Yannick Fontan
fullText.text:
Symbolic Reasoning Agent
An experimental journey through ARC-AGI 3
Episode 4 • Official Game FT09
Observing and Verbalizing Reasoning

Today, I would like to challenge another common assumption: that certain puzzles are solved by intuition rather than by reasoning.

When people solve a difficult problem, they often cannot explain how they reached their conclusion. Asked to describe their reasoning, they simply answer that it was intuition. I believe this is often misleading. It reveals not the absence of reasoning, but the difficulty of consciously observing it while it unfolds.

In environments such as ARC 3, reasoning combines geometric perception, logical inference, analogies and hypothesis testing within a fraction of a second. Because these operations are highly compressed and rarely verbalized, they appear as intuition when they are actually the result of genuine symbolic reasoning.

This is where consciousness makes a profound difference. Beyond maintaining the state of what matters, it also allows us to observe our own cognitive activity. The more accurately we observe our reasoning, the more faithfully we can verbalize it. Only then can it be examined, refined and transmitted.

This ability can be cultivated. With practice, implicit reasoning gradually becomes explicit, revealing symbolic structures that were always present but remained outside the reach of language.

Before teaching the machine, the human must first learn to observe and verbalize his own reasoning. Only then does Human-Agent Principle Distillation become meaningful, because a principle cannot be distilled until the reasoning that produced it has been made explicit.

Making reasoning explicit is therefore much more than an exercise in explanation. It transforms a personal cognitive process into knowledge that can be inspected, challenged, shared and eventually transmitted to another intelligence. I believe this ability will become one of the essential foundations of future symbolic reasoning systems.

"Every reasoning that can be faithfully verbalized becomes knowledge that can be transmitted."

videos.title: ARC AGI 3 SRA Ep 5
videos.summary: VC33 provides the setting for a discussion of alignment. Here the term includes expectations that a world has coherent rules, conventions that make objects recognizable, and assumptions about its designer’s intentions. Yannick examines when an acquired principle deserves continued use, and how consistency can support that trust. The episode connects these expectations to the symbols, goals, and values supplied by the people developing an intelligent system.

fullText.author: Yannick Fontan
fullText.text:
Symbolic Reasoning Agent
An experimental journey through ARC-AGI 3
Episode 5 • Game VC33
Reasoning Begins with Alignment

Last time, I argued that what we often perceive as intuition is, in many cases, a genuine reasoning process that has simply been misinterpreted because it remained outside conscious observation and verbalization.

Today, I would like to challenge another common assumption: we often think reasoning begins with logic, while I believe it begins much earlier, with alignment.

In the physical world, identical causes usually produce identical consequences. We rarely question this because the universe itself appears remarkably coherent. Video games are different. Every rule is artificial. A designer could decide that gravity changes every minute, that oxygen sometimes increases instead of decreasing, or that a key opens a different door every time it is used.

Yet almost no game behaves this way.

Not because it would be impossible, but because it would no longer make sense. We expect consistency. We expect coherent rules. We expect the world to remain understandable as we explore it. These expectations are not produced by logic. They already exist before reasoning begins.

This is already a form of alignment.

But alignment goes even further. It is also cultural.

A key opens a lock. Red often suggests danger. Green often suggests safety. Treasure rewards exploration. Walls remain solid. None of these relationships are dictated by physics. They are conventions inherited from a shared culture between the designer and the player. Because we are aligned with that culture, we immediately recognize meanings that would otherwise require countless experiments to rediscover.

Alignment is therefore not only physical.

It is also cultural.

And beyond culture, it is moral.

A game designer could still change the rules randomly, punish the player without cause, or invalidate everything previously learned. Nothing prevents this from a technical point of view. Yet we generally reject such designs because we expect fairness, coherence and respect for the player's effort. These expectations are moral standards before they become technical ones, and they provide intelligence with something invaluable: the confidence that what has been learned deserves to remain meaningful.

This is why I believe reasoning begins with alignment. Logic allows us to explore the consequences of accepted principles, but it does not tell us which principles deserve our trust, which meanings are shared, or why the world itself should remain coherent. Those assumptions are inherited before logic begins to operate.

An intelligent agent should therefore not endlessly retest principles that have repeatedly demonstrated their coherence. Once a principle has been validated, intelligence consists not only in remembering it, but also in trusting that the world continues to respect it. This trust is not blind. It reflects an alignment with the intentions that give the world its meaning.

I believe this idea extends far beyond video games. No created intelligence can escape the meaningfulness it inherits from the perspective of its creator. Every created intelligence understands its world through principles, symbols, objectives and values that it did not invent itself. The more deeply it understands the intentions behind those foundations, the more insight it gains into why the world is the way it is. Alignment therefore becomes more than a source of efficiency. It becomes a source of understanding, practical intelligence and, ultimately, wisdom.

"Reasoning does not begin with logic. It begins with alignment."

videos.displayTitle: The Search for the Primitives of Reasoning
videos.summary: The sixth episode, set in AR25, separates stored knowledge, cognitive transformations, and the workflows that organize them. Terms and claims express structural, dynamic, epistemic, and control relations. Yannick proposes nine operators: OBSERVE, ACT, DISTINGUISH, RELATE, PROPOSE, DERIVE, COMPARE, UPDATE, and SELECT. He uses TEST as an example of a workflow built from such operations, with principles determining when a step is justified. The vocabulary is a working proposal; some transformations remain within specialized capabilities, and the operator set may change.

fullText.author: Yannick Fontan
fullText.text:
Symbolic Reasoning Agent
Episode 6 • Game AR25
The Search for the Primitives of Reasoning

Across mathematics, engineering, medicine, language and artificial intelligence, every domain has developed its own reasoning principles and methodologies. Yet we still lack a widely accepted description of the elementary mechanisms shared across these fields.
This raises a fundamental question:
What is reasoning actually made of?
My first attempt begins by separating what an intelligence stores, the transformations it performs and the workflows that organize them.
At its core, the system stores terms and claims.
A term represents something the intelligence can think about: an entity, event, schema, procedure, goal or value. A claim connects terms by expressing something observed, inferred, possible, contradicted or provisionally accepted.
These claims describe four families of relations.
Structural relations describe what things are and how they are organized.
Dynamic relations describe events, transformations and causes.
Epistemic relations preserve evidence, alternatives, contradictions and deductions.
Control relations connect knowledge to goals, constraints and decisions.
But storing knowledge is not reasoning. In this architecture, reasoning begins when the stored symbolic structure is transformed. 
The current agent uses nine candidate cognitive operators, grouped into four families.
The first family grounds intelligence in the world. OBSERVE transforms incoming information into events and claims, while ACT intentionally changes the environment.
The second family constructs meaning. DISTINGUISH separates elements according to a criterion. RELATE creates explicit connections between them. PROPOSE introduces a possible interpretation, goal, procedure or principle without treating it as established knowledge.
The third family tests knowledge. DERIVE produces consequences from existing claims and declared rules. COMPARE evaluates observations, predictions or competing explanations according to a stated criterion.
The final family regulates reasoning. UPDATE revises claims after new evidence has been assessed. SELECT chooses among eligible actions, hypotheses or strategies according to goals, constraints and guiding principles.
These operators form a cognitive vocabulary, but they do not organize reasoning by themselves.
Operators describe what cognitive transformation takes place. Workflows describe how transformations are organized through time. Principles describe the conditions under which a transformation, conclusion or decision is justified. 
Consider the workflow TEST.
Testing a hypothesis requires the intelligence to select a discriminating experiment, act upon the world, observe the result, compare it with the expected effect and update the relevant claims:
SELECT → ACT → OBSERVE → COMPARE → UPDATE
TEST is therefore not an additional primitive. It is a reusable composition that can appear in scientific experimentation, medical diagnosis, software investigation or the exploration of an unfamiliar environment.
Other workflows can track an entity, propagate a change through dependent relations, construct a plan, preserve competing explanations or commit to an action.
Principles answer a different question: what makes a reasoning step justified? A principle specifies the premises, conditions and constraints supporting a conclusion, revision or decision, as well as the evidence that would invalidate it. 
A workflow may apply several principles, and the same principle may guide different workflows.
At this stage, my architecture remains experimental and incomplete: Observation, action, derivation, comparison, revision and selection are already explicit throughout the active reasoning process. Other transformations — particularly distinguishing entities and constructing relations — are still sometimes performed implicitly inside specialized capabilities.
The objective is not to preserve this particular list of operators. Some may eventually merge, disappear or be decomposed further. The goal is to identify the smallest useful set of transformations capable of describing how an intelligence observes, interprets, tests, revises and acts across many domains.
Making these transformations explicit would allow an artificial intelligence to communicate not only its conclusions, but also what it observed, proposed, derived, compared, revised and selected—and which principles justified those decisions.
The current agent does not yet prove that all reasoning can be reduced to these primitives. It demonstrates something more modest but already valuable: complex reasoning can often be reconstructed as an understandable composition of a limited cognitive vocabulary, explicit principles and inspectable workflows.

The search for universal cognitive primitives may therefore offer a path toward artificial intelligence whose reasoning can be understood, challenged, taught and progressively improved.
